First, there are two kinds of churches recognized under federal tax code. There are "free" churches (508c1) that can pretty much do whatever they want. The statute grants them an exception to pay, or even file tax returns. There are virtually no restrictions on what these churches can say, or do politically (They can outright endorse political candidates, etc. ) because, aside from granting the exception for taxation, the code only says that they must not a private foundation and the gross receipts (taxable) for each year are normally not more than $5,000.

So, if you don't have more than $5000 profit annually, you can be a 508c1 church and say whatever you want.

Then, there are 501c3 "incorporated" churches. These are churches that for whatever reason, have decided to seek status with the federal government by either incorporating into an operating company, or forming a charitable group, etc. 501c3's have to meet a set of federal requirements in order to be granted a tax exempt status. Straight from the IRS code:

  • To be tax-exempt under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code, an organization must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes set forth in section 501(c)(3), and none of its earnings may inure to any private shareholder or individual. In addition, it may not be an action organization, i.e., it may not attempt to influence legislation as a substantial part of its activities and it may not participate in any campaign activity for or against political candidates.

These churches are technically required by law to 1) restrict political speech 2) hold any income generated internally, or use it within the organization

This is where you have churches like "The Inspiring Body of Christ Church", who built a $4.7million private aquarium, or churches buying private planes for pastors.
